name: Manifest destiny
summary: Manifest destiny was the mid-nineteenth-century American belief that the United States was providentially destined to spread across the continent and extend republican self-government, a phrase coined by John L. O'Sullivan in 1845 and linked by the reference works to the Polk administration's annexation of Texas, the Oregon settlement and the Mexican war. It combined democratic equality among settlers, a mission to the world and claims of racial and cultural superiority, and the record is the displacement of Native American nations and the taking of Mexican lands.
scope: The mid-nineteenth-century expansionist belief as the reference and scholarly works define it (Hidalgo's and Scholnick's Encyclopedia.com entries and the American Yawp chapter), read through O'Sullivan's essays of 1839 and 1845, which those works tie to it by title. His other writings, such as his 1837 statement of the democratic principle, are not the doctrine's: the sources present manifest destiny as a belief he named, not his body of thought (coatrack correction, 2026-11-14). It excludes the later overseas imperialism of 1898 and Wilsonian internationalism, which the sources treat as later expressions, and Polk's own views on tariffs, banks and the Union, which are Jacksonian Democratic positions, not the doctrine's. It was never a fixed programme, so most economic, family and social statements stay null.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay calls the principle of privilege unnatural and destructive, and the aristocracy of blood a prejudice of other times that the American masses will not venerate.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay condemns public debts as the pawning of the people's property and labour.

clerical-rule.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay names the theocracy of priests among the relics of other times and says America's example will smite the tyranny of hierarchs.

consent-of-governed.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay rests the right of Texas and California settlers on their natural right of self-government, and the editor notes Texas entered by a citizen vote and expansion was to end in voluntary accession.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Hidalgo and Scholnick report that believers held their economic system and culture to be the most developed and their people the most advanced, with a divine right to acquire and dominate.

democracy-best.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay holds that a nation's happiness, greatness and duration are proportionate to the democratic equality in its government, though it also warns of the despotism of the majority.

divinely-chosen-superior-people.rationale: Hidalgo says believers held the United States preordained by God to expand and exercise hegemony over its neighbours as the most advanced race, and O'Sullivan's 1839 essay says America has been chosen for its mission to the nations.

dynastic-succession.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay rejects the monarchy of one and the aristocracy of blood as unnatural, and says the nation 'owns no man master'.

elective-rulers.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay rejects the monarchy of one and holds that a nation's greatness is proportionate to democratic equality in its government.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Hidalgo reports that expansion created a permanent economic and cultural underclass of Native Americans and Hispanics, and the Yawp that it rested on removal and a belief that white Americans could best use the land, so the record did not give all people equal rights.

free-trade.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay names freedom of trade and business pursuits among the principles of America's mission.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Hidalgo says its believers held that Providence or genetics had preordained the people of the United States and that they belonged to the most advanced race, and the Yawp says its champions grafted biological imperatives onto American political culture.

homestead-ownership.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay says settlers have a better and truer right to the homes they conquered from the wilderness by their own labour than Mexico's inherited title of sovereignty.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Hidalgo reports that most of the territorial growth came at the expense of the Native American nations, and the Yawp that expansion hinged on a policy of Indian removal; the record is dispossession.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The record is settlers organising republican governments and territories over lands taken from Native American nations and Mexicans, who became a permanent underclass in Hidalgo's account.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay says the principle on which a nation is organised fixes its destiny, and traces decline to forms of government, not to the economic structure.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay treats monarchy, the divine right of kings and the aristocracy of blood as relics America will leave behind, which leaves no place for hereditary rulers, though he does not discuss a purely ceremonial one.

national-mission.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay says the nation is destined to manifest divine principles to mankind and that America's high example will smite the tyranny of kings and hierarchs, and the Yawp reads him as stating a God-given mission to lead the world to democracy.

national-self-determination.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay says the natural right of self-government belongs to any community distinct in position, origin and character that is strong enough to maintain it.

no-business-privileges.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay calls privilege destructive and has corporate privileges shrinking before individual rights.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay rejects the aristocracy of blood and says the nation 'owns no man master', which excludes rule resting on personal loyalty to lords.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay makes spreading democratic equality to the nations under tyranny America's mission, and the editor's note to the 1845 essay says its supporters wanted to support European revolutions actively; he leans on example more than on force.

race-social-construct.rationale: Hidalgo and the Yawp describe the doctrine as resting on a belief in a superior, biologically advanced race, the opposite of treating racial categories as constructs.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: The Yawp says expansion hinged on a federal policy of Indian removal, and Hidalgo that growth came at the expense of the Native American nations, so removal was part of the record.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay holds that Mexico's breach of its federal compact with the Texans justified resistance and independence.

restore-past-order.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay says the nation's birth 'separates us from the past and connects us with the future only' and calls it the nation of progress that cannot retrograde.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The record is opening native lands to settlement by removal and war, as the Yawp and Hidalgo report, the opposite of restricting outside settlement there.

right-to-secede.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay says a community distinct in position, origin and character and strong enough to hold its own has a natural right to self-government free of its old political body, as with Texas and California against Mexico.

sacred-nation.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1845 essay calls the nation 'Our Country', a sacred designation, and says patriotism thrills for Texas as part of la patrie.

sacred-ruler.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay lists the divine right of kings among the superstitions the American people will not venerate.

state-harmful.rationale: O'Sullivan's mission is to extend a Union of republics with constitutions and legislatures over the continent, which a call to abolish the state would contradict.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay names freedom of trade among the principles of America's mission.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hidalgo records that the United States grew by about 1.2 million square miles, more than 60 percent, through Texas, Oregon and the Mexican cession, mostly at the expense of Mexico and the Native American nations, and the Yawp says expansion hinged on removal and wars with native peoples and foreign nations; the record answers.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay says Americans have little connection with the past history of any nation and still less with antiquity, and that the national birth was the beginning of a new history.

universal-morality.rationale: O'Sullivan's 1839 essay grounds equality in a principle that is 'perfect' and 'universal', the self-evident dictate of morality that defines the duty of man to man.

missingStatements.text: My country has a special mission to spread its form of government to other peoples.
missingStatements.rationale: O'Sullivan presents America as a nation of destiny that will spread democratic equality and 'smite unto death the tyranny of kings'; historians call a unique mission central to the belief.

notes: Themes searched in the saved sources: territory and expansion, race and the Native American nations, the Mexican war and conquest, monarchy and hereditary privilege, democracy and consent, religion and providence, progress and the past, privilege and corporations, and foreign interference. The defining sources say nothing on welfare, taxes, family, gender, the environment, technology, most civil liberties and most government statements, which stay null. Polk's 1845 inaugural address, 1845 and 1846 annual messages and 1846 war message were read (saved locally) but the defining sources do not tie them to the doctrine by title, and his tariff, bank and Union positions are Jacksonian Democratic views, so earlier answers resting on them were nulled. Supporters split on peaceful annexation and conquest and on slavery's extension; the sources record both and no statement here rests on one side. A pass against rules 7 re-checked every earlier answer. Direct fetches of the Teaching American History pages were refused (Cloudflare) and not retried; Wayback copies were used. Brought up to rules 7 on 2026-11-13.
